title: object oriented programming
summary: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a foundational programming paradigm based on the concept of objects containing data fields and associated procedures.
subject: Computer Science

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a dominant software design paradigm centered around objects rather than isolated logic or functions. Originating with languages like Simula in the 1960s and popularized by Smalltalk, C++, and Java, OOP revolutionized how developers structure complex software. Objects act as self-contained units that combine data fields with executable methods. Today, OOP principles are incorporated into major multi-paradigm languages, including Python, C#, and JavaScript.

sections.heading: Core Pillars of OOP
sections.body: The architecture of OOP rests on four fundamental principles: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism. Encapsulation ensures that internal object states are protected from unauthorized external modification by bundling data with relevant procedures. Abstraction simplifies software complexity by exposing only necessary user interfaces while concealing intricate background logic. Inheritance allows developers to reuse code across hierarchies, while polymorphism enables identical method signatures to execute context-specific logic across different classes.

sections.heading: Design Patterns and SOLID Principles
sections.body: To maintain scalable OOP systems, software engineers rely on established architectural guidelines such as the SOLID principles. Introduced by Robert C. Martin, these five principles advocate for single-responsibility components, open-closed extensions, and interface segregation. Furthermore, standardized design patterns like the Factory, Singleton, and Observer patterns provide proven solutions to recurring structural challenges. Following these conventions minimizes software rigidity and reduces technical debt over long-term project lifecycles.

sections.heading: Real-World Application
sections.body: Modern enterprise software relies heavily on OOP to construct maintainable, modular systems. For instance, Graphical User Interface (GUI) frameworks represent screen elements like buttons, text fields, and windows as distinct objects with properties and event handlers. Video game engines also utilize OOP to model dynamic entities, such as player characters, non-player enemies, and environmental assets. By mirroring real-world entities, object-oriented systems allow engineering teams to collaborate seamlessly on massive software projects.
